mac_awake.mac_reference_basis: each patient's own age-adjusted MAC (Katoh 1993, slow washout, descending)

sources.citation: De Wolf AM, Van Zundert TC, De Cooman S, Hendrickx JF. Theoretical effect of hyperventilation on speed of recovery and risk of rehypnotization following recovery - a Gas Man simulation. BMC Anesthesiology. 2012;12:22.
sources.note: Tier 3, reference implementation (see docs/MODEL.md, 'Source hierarchy'). Table 1 reports the Gas Man sevoflurane blood:gas and tissue:gas coefficients used here. De Wolf et al. ran Gas Man simulations and measured no coefficient: Table 1 is the parameter set they supplied to it, so this is the Gas Man set carrying a journal's name rather than a measurement. It is the source of the stored values.

sources.citation: Strum DP, Eger EI II. Partition coefficients for sevoflurane in human blood, saline, and olive oil. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 1987;66(7):654-656.
sources.note: Tier 1, primary measurement, cited but not adopted. Human study reporting a blood:gas coefficient of 0.686 +/- 0.047 (mean +/- SD) at 37 degrees C in 19 ASA I-III patients aged 21-77. The stored value 0.65 is the Gas Man figure and is 5.2 percent lower. No primary source has been adopted for this parameter; PL-D6LX carries the decision.

sources.citation: Yasuda N, Targ AG, Eger EI II. Solubility of I-653, sevoflurane, isoflurane, and halothane in human tissues. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 1989;69(3):370-373.
sources.note: Tier 1, primary measurement, cited but not adopted. Human tissue study reporting a sevoflurane brain:blood partition coefficient of 1.70 +/- 0.09 at 37 degrees C. The stored tissue:gas values are Gas Man's; dividing vessel_rich by blood:gas gives an implied brain:blood of 1.1/0.65 = 1.692, 0.5 percent below Yasuda's measurement. Adopting the measured values is not a substitution: this model's vessel_rich group is a lumped compartment (brain, heart, liver, kidney, viscera) and Yasuda reports per-organ coefficients, so a group-weighting scheme would have to be constructed and justified. PL-D6LX carries that. WHAT THE GAS MAN WORKBOOK ATTRIBUTES, RECORDED 2026-09-13 (PL-ZP7Z). The note printed beneath the Workbook's page-168 Model Parameters table reads, in these words: 'Values for nitrous oxide and enflurane are taken from Eger, 1981. Values for isoflurane, halothane, desflurane and sevoflurane are taken from Yasuda, Targ and Eger. Values for nitrogen are taken from Weathersby and Homer, 1980. Values for sevoflurane are taken from the package insert and Abbott data.' Read at the source 2026-09-06 from the copy the project owner supplied. So Gas Man says its volatile coefficients ARE this paper's authors', which is a stronger relationship than 'cited but not adopted' conveys on its own, and is why this block was written. IT NAMES A DIFFERENT DOCUMENT FROM THE ONE CITED HERE, AND THAT IS THE FIRST THING TO GET RIGHT. The Workbook's reference 45 is 'Anesthesiology 69:A615' - an American Society of Anesthesiologists annual-meeting abstract in the 1988 supplement - not the 1989 Anesthesia & Analgesia paper this entry cites. An abstract and a full paper are not interchangeable sources: the abstract carries no methods and no full table. Nor is it reachable by this project's route: a PubMed search for the Yasuda, Targ and Eger tissue-solubility work in Anesthesiology returned nothing on 2026-09-13, as a meeting-abstract supplement does. What that abstract reports, and whether it differs from the paper, is unknown here and is left recorded as unknown rather than assumed identical. Note also that the two volumes collide by coincidence - Anesthesiology volume 69 is 1988 and Anesthesia & Analgesia volume 69 is 1989 - so 'Yasuda 69' alone identifies neither. THE ARITHMETIC SAYS THE ATTRIBUTION IS CLOSE, AND SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE ROUTE. This paper's measured brain:blood of 1.70 times this file's stored blood:gas of 0.65 is 1.1050, which is the stored vessel-rich tissue:gas of 1.1 at the precision the file keeps. Desflurane's behaves the same way (1.29 x 0.42 = 0.5418 against a stored 0.54); isoflurane's does not (1.57 x 1.3 = 2.0410 against a stored 2.1, which 2.04 does not round to). Two of the three stored vessel-rich figures are reproduced exactly and the third is missed by 2.9 percent - still inside half the measurement's own standard deviation. That is evidence the route is roughly right, not evidence of what the route was. THE CHECK THAT WOULD SETTLE IT CANNOT BE RUN FROM ANYTHING THIS PROJECT HOLDS, AND THAT IS THE REAL GAP. The stored coefficients are tissue:GAS; the 1989 paper's abstract reports tissue:BLOOD only, which is why the comparison above has to go through a blood:gas the Workbook's sentence does not attribute to Yasuda at all. The full paper reports both. Yasuda et al. 1991 (Comparison of kinetics of sevoflurane and isoflurane in humans, Anesth Analg 1991;72:316-24, PMID 1994760), read at full text from the private reference corpus 2026-09-13, cites it as its own source for 'the tissue/blood partition coefficient (which we determined previously)' and, in the same paragraph, for 'the tissue/gas partition coefficient'. So the one comparison that would settle this - Yasuda 1989's published tissue:gas values against the twelve stored across these three files - needs that paper's full text. It is not in PubMed Central and it is not among the corpus's holdings, so the route ends there. PL-ZP7Z carries the request to the project owner, naming the tables needed. THIS AGENT IS THE ONE THE WORKBOOK CREDITS TWICE, AND THE TWO CREDITS DISAGREE. The same paragraph says the sevoflurane values are Yasuda, Targ and Eger's, and then says they are 'taken from the package insert and Abbott data' - Abbott marketed sevoflurane as Ultane. A manufacturer's package insert is not a measurement anybody here has read either, and it is a different document from a tissue-solubility study. Whichever of the two the Workbook meant, one of its own sentences is wrong about where these four numbers came from, which is on its own enough to keep them at tier 3. It also explains something this file already recorded without an explanation: the stored sevoflurane tissue:blood ratios sit within half a percent of this paper's measurement, which had read as a near-coincidence and now reads as a partial attribution nobody can finish checking. THE TIER DOES NOT CHANGE, AND WOULD NOT CHANGE EVEN IF THE ATTRIBUTION WERE CONFIRMED. This entry stays tier 1, not adopted; the stored coefficients stay De Wolf et al. 2012's table, tier 3, adopted. Three reasons, the first sufficient on its own. A program's statement about its own provenance is the program talking, and docs/MODEL.md, 'Source hierarchy', turns on what a value descends from - the same rule that stops De Wolf's journal name from promoting the table it prints. The Workbook's own paragraph contradicts itself for sevoflurane, crediting it to Yasuda and, one sentence later, to the package insert and Abbott data. And whatever it took from Yasuda it took at an unstated rounding, through an unattributed blood:gas, from a document nobody here has read. What WOULD change the tier is reading Yasuda 1989 and finding the stored twelve in its tables.

sources.citation: Drager Vapor 2000 Sevoflurane vaporizer specification: calibrated concentration range 0.2-8%.
sources.note: Manufacturer specification, and the primary source for a device capability: docs/MODEL.md's source hierarchy concerns measured physiologic quantities, and a calibrated dial maximum is not one. Standard variable-bypass sevoflurane vaporizer (e.g. Drager Vapor 2000, Datex-Ohmeda Sevotec 5) calibrated dial maximum, used here as max_delivered_concentration_percent. This is a device-capability limit on the delivered-concentration control, not a scientific model parameter; it does not affect the governing equations.

sources.citation: Nickalls RWD, Mapleson WW. Age-related iso-MAC charts for isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane in man. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 2003;91(2):170-174.
sources.note: The stored mac_percent is tier 3: it is the flat adult MAC De Wolf et al. state they used in their Gas Man simulations, not a value taken from this paper. Nickalls and Mapleson is cited but not adopted. It is tier 2, not tier 1 - its own abstract states the charts "are based on Mapleson's meta-analysis (1996) of the available MAC data", so it synthesises measurements rather than making one, and docs/MODEL.md's source hierarchy admits a tier-2 source as the authority for a stored value only on a recorded decision, and none has been taken for this parameter. It is also age-related, and this project's reference-adult model has no age parameter, so mac_percent uses the flat adult value from De Wolf et al. above (same paper already cited for partition coefficients: 'MAC values that we used in our Gas Man simulations are: desflurane 6%, sevoflurane 2%, isoflurane 1.2%'). Used as the controller's starting delivered-concentration default (1 MAC) and as the divisor of the interface's MAC-multiple display unit; it is not a governing-equation parameter and no equation in core/ reads it. See docs/MODEL.md, 'MAC multiples as a display unit' and 'Delivery-limit and MAC parameters'.

sources.citation: Mapleson WW. Effect of age on MAC in humans: a meta-analysis. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 1996;76(2):179-185.
sources.note: Tier 2, secondary synthesis, cited but not adopted; the source of the age-40 MAC this project's stored value is measured against. Regression of a comprehensive literature survey, reporting MAC at age 40 as 1.8 percent for sevoflurane (95% confidence limits about plus or minus 7 percent for isoflurane and sevoflurane and 10 percent for desflurane), and MAC falling about 6 percent per decade of age. The stored mac_percent of 2 percent is 11.1 percent higher. Not adopted for two reasons: a meta-analysis measures nothing and is tier 2 under docs/MODEL.md's source hierarchy, which admits a tier-2 source as the authority only on a recorded decision, and this one was decided the other way on 2026-09-04; and every other parameter in this model is the Gas Man set, so a Mapleson divisor over a Gas Man trajectory would make each displayed MAC multiple a ratio between two parameter lineages. The consequence is displayed and disclosed rather than silently absorbed: against this source the interface's MAC multiples for sevoflurane read 10 percent low, and because the sevoflurane and desflurane errors run in opposite directions a cross-agent comparison at '1 MAC' is displaced by about 22 percent. docs/MODEL.md, 'Known limitations', carries that; ROADMAP.md's planned-milestone item 31 is the route to primary values.

sources.citation: Katoh T, Suguro Y, Kimura T, Ikeda K. Cerebral awakening concentration of sevoflurane and isoflurane predicted during slow and fast alveolar washout. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 1993;77(5):1012-1017.
sources.note: Tier 1, primary measurement, and the source of the stored mac_awake. 49 ASA I patients; MAC-awake was determined as the average of the bracketing alveolar concentrations that allow and prevent response to verbal command during recovery, and reported "as a ratio to age-adjusted MAC". That ratio is what is stored: it is the form the paper reports, and the only form that stays correct if mac_percent is ever changed or made age-aware. Slow washout (concentration decreased in 15-minute steps, brain assumed equilibrated with alveolar gas) gave 0.34 +/- 0.05 for sevoflurane; fast washout (discontinuation from 0.5 MAC) gave 0.22 +/- 0.07 MAC, significantly smaller, and the paper attributes the difference to end-tidal-to-arterial and arterial-to-cerebral anesthetic differences - which is what this model represents as the alveolar-to-vessel-rich difference. The slow-washout figure is the one stored because it is the *brain* concentration at awakening, and the paper measures that directly rather than leaving it to inference: cerebral concentration at first eye opening during fast washout was 0.34 +/- 0.08 MAC, "nearly equal to MAC-Awake obtained by slow alveolar washout". That is why docs/MODEL.md requires the band to be read against the vessel-rich trace. Determination is descending (during washout); the desflurane value in desflurane.json is ascending, and the two are not interchangeable methods. Retrieved from PubMed (PMID 8214700) and verified against the abstract 2026-09-04.

provenance_gap: No primary measurement is adopted for this agent's blood:gas coefficient, its three tissue:gas coefficients, or mac_percent. All four coefficients are the Gas Man parameter set as published in De Wolf et al. 2012 - tier 3, reference implementation - and mac_percent is the flat adult MAC that paper states it used in its Gas Man simulations. The primary measurements are cited above and explicitly not adopted; each of those notes records the measured value, its reference conditions, and how far the stored number sits from it. Two parameters in this file DO carry an adopted primary source - mac_awake (Katoh 1993) and max_delivered_concentration_percent (the vaporizer's calibrated maximum) - so this gap is specific to the coefficients and the MAC divisor rather than to the file as a whole. The decision to keep the Gas Man values and label them, rather than move to the primary figures, was taken by the project owner on 2026-09-03 (PL-D6LX); ROADMAP.md's planned-milestone item 31 is the route to a primary-literature coefficient set. See docs/MODEL.md, 'Source hierarchy'. The Gas Man Workbook attributes these coefficients to Yasuda, Targ and Eger; what that does and does not establish - and why it leaves the tier where it is - is in the Yasuda entry above (PL-ZP7Z, 2026-09-13).
